git__additions.name: Addition Count (Last {days} Days)
git__additions.short: Number of lines of code added to this file or component in the last {days} days.
git__additions.long: Counts how many new lines of code were added in git commits over the last {days} days. Helps identify recently active or growing files.

git__deletions.name: Deletion Count (Last {days} Days)
git__deletions.short: Number of lines of code deleted from this file or component in the last {days} days.
git__deletions.long: Counts how many lines of code were deleted in git commits over the last {days} days. Helps identify recently refactored or cleaned-up files.

git__commits.name: Commit Count (Last {days} Days)
git__commits.short: Number of unique git commits modifying this file or component in the last {days} days.
git__commits.long: Counts how many times this file or component was modified in a git commit over the last {days} days. A high count suggests a recent hot spot of activity.

git__authors.name: Author Count (Last {days} Days)
git__authors.short: Number of unique authors who modified this file or component in the last {days} days.
git__authors.long: Counts how many different developers made changes to this file or component in the last {days} days. High author count can indicate a risk of coordination issues.

git__unique_file_changes.name: Unique File Changes (Last {days} Days)
git__unique_file_changes.short: Number of unique files changed in commits that touched this file or component in the last {days} days.
git__unique_file_changes.long: Measures co-changes over the last {days} days: how many other files were modified in the same commits as this one. Helps find implicit logical coupling.

app__components.name: Components
app__components.short: Components in the snapshot, the root excluded.
app__components.long: Every component the scan grouped files into. The root component ('.') holds files outside every other component and is left out, as it is on every screen.

app__components_in_tangles.name: Components in tangles
app__components_in_tangles.short: Components that sit in a dependency cycle with at least one other.
app__components_in_tangles.long: A tangle is a strongly connected group of two or more components: each can reach every other by following imports. Components in a tangle cannot be released, tested or understood apart from the rest of it.

app__cross_component_edges.name: Component dependencies
app__cross_component_edges.short: Ordered pairs of components where one imports the other.
app__cross_component_edges.long: Distinct (from, to) pairs in the direct connections, the root excluded. A pair counts once however many imports it carries.

app__dependency_levels.name: Dependency levels
app__dependency_levels.short: Layers in the dependency graph once tangles are collapsed.
app__dependency_levels.long: Collapse each tangle into one node, then count the nodes on the longest import chain. A tall stack with few tangles is a layered system; a short stack with one large tangle is not.
app__dependency_levels.method: Longest path in the condensation of component_connections_direct, computed in the app.

app__largest_tangle.name: Largest tangle
app__largest_tangle.long: The size of the largest strongly connected group. One big tangle is a different problem from many small ones: it usually means the system has no layers left.

app__last_changed_days.name: Days since last change
app__last_changed_days.short: Days since a file last changed, counted back to the snapshot's head commit.
app__last_changed_days.long: Counted back from the newest commit in the scan, not from today, so a snapshot says the same thing whenever it is read. A pure rename is not a change: a moved file keeps its age. A component takes its most recently changed file's. Engine revision 2 records this per file as git__last_change_age_in_days; older snapshots are computed in the app from git_commits (anchored at scan time).

app__lines_in_tangles_share.name: Lines in tangles
app__lines_in_tangles_share.short: Share of all lines of code that sit in a tangle.
app__lines_in_tangles_share.long: Lines of the components in a tangle over the lines of all components. A count of components understates a tangle of large components; this weighs them by size.

app__median_distance.name: Median distance from the main sequence
app__median_distance.long: The median of modularity__distance_main_sequence over components. Read with care in languages without explicit abstractions (Python, JavaScript, Go), where abstractness is near zero for everything.

app__median_instability.name: Median instability
app__median_instability.short: The middle component's instability, Ce / (Ca + Ce).
app__median_instability.long: The median of modularity__instability over components. Half the components are more stable than this, half less. The median ignores the handful of leaf and root components that pull the mean to the ends.

app__propagation_cost.name: Propagation cost
app__propagation_cost.short: Share of component pairs where a change in one can reach the other: (reachable pairs + N) / N².
app__propagation_cost.long: MacCormack's propagation cost: the ordered pairs (a, b) where a reaches b through imports, directly or not, plus the N pairs of each component with itself, over the number of components squared. Near 0, changes stay local; past about 0.4, most changes can ripple through most of the system. Pairs are counted once: the snapshot's table can repeat a row.

app__rule_findings.name: Rule findings
app__rule_findings.short: Imports that break a dependency rule.
app__rule_findings.long: Rows of the rules table with status 'violation': each is one import, in one file, at one line, that a configured rule forbids.

app__test_importers.name: Test files importing it
app__test_importers.short: Test files, in any component, that import this component.
app__test_importers.long: Distinct files with role 'test' among the direct connections into a component. A component no test file imports is tested, if at all, only through something else.

codesmells__bumpy_road.name: Bumpy Road
codesmells__bumpy_road.long: Calculates the density of indentation changes by summing absolute differences in indentation levels between consecutive lines, normalized by the count of non-empty lines. High values point to high cognitive load and code paths going in and out of nested structures. Component score represents size-weighted volatility.

codesmells__code_health.name: Code Health
codesmells__code_health.short: A rating from 1.0 to 10.0 of how costly a file's code is to change, read from the code alone.
codesmells__code_health.long:
10 less three deductions, never below 1. Complex code: a point per doubling of the lines inside functions whose cognitive complexity passes 15, counted as 1 + lines ÷ 25. Coupling: a point and a half per doubling of import statements past 10. Size: a point per doubling of code lines past 150. Each was kept for predicting later bug fixes beyond what size predicts, on fifteen codebases read as they stood two years earlier; indentation was dropped for predicting nothing beyond size.

A file in a programming language no language pack parses is read by its indentation instead: size from its non-blank lines past 180, and a point per doubling of 1 + lines three levels in ÷ 25. Markup, data, stylesheets, SQL and shell scripts get no reading.

A component's or directory's health is its files' weighted by code lines, with its least healthy file beside it.

codesmells__code_health__worst_file.name: Least healthy file
codesmells__code_health__worst_file.short: The lowest code health among a component's or directory's files.
codesmells__code_health__worst_file.long: Shown beside the group's health, which is its files' weighted by code lines and can hide one bad file among many good ones. Not recorded for single files.

codesmells__health__deduction__complex_c.name: Complex code deduction
codesmells__health__deduction__complex_c.short: Points taken off a file's health for the lines inside functions whose cognitive complexity passes 15.
codesmells__health__deduction__complex_c.long: One point per doubling of 1 + those lines ÷ 25: 25 lines cost a point, 75 two, 175 three. Edits to long, complex functions were bug fixes about 1.6 times as often as edits to equally long simple ones; long simple functions were no worse than short ones. The functions view names them. Recorded for parsed files only.

codesmells__health__deduction__coupling.name: Coupling deduction
codesmells__health__deduction__coupling.short: Points taken off a file's health for its imports: one and a half per doubling past 10.
codesmells__health__deduction__coupling.long: 20 imports cost a point and a half, 40 three. Every import counts, the standard library's and other projects' too: what the file has to know about predicted later fixes, where the files it reaches inside the project did not. Recorded for parsed files only.

codesmells__health__deduction__deep_code.name: Deep code deduction
codesmells__health__deduction__deep_code.short: For a file no pack parses: points taken off its health for lines indented three levels or more.
codesmells__health__deduction__deep_code.long: One point per doubling of 1 + those lines ÷ 25. The indentation stand-in for complex code in a language without a pack, scored as if the fifteen tested codebases had no parser: weaker than reading functions, but better than the average or deepest indentation the score used before.

codesmells__health__deduction__size.name: Size deduction
codesmells__health__deduction__size.short: Points taken off a file's health for its size: one per doubling of code lines past 150.
codesmells__health__deduction__size.long: 300 code lines cost one point, 600 two, 1,200 three; nothing caps it. A file no pack parsed is measured by its non-blank lines past 180 instead. Bigger files collect more bug fixes, though not more per line, so this deduction is about how much there is to change rather than how well it is written. Recorded for files only.

codesmells__hotspot__raw.name: Raw hotspot
codesmells__hotspot__raw.short: log2(commits + 1) × lines, before it is scaled to 0–100 against the hottest file.
codesmells__hotspot__raw.long: The hotspot score is this number as a share of the largest one in the snapshot, times 100, so it only compares files within one scan. The raw value can be compared across scans of the same code. A component or directory carries its hottest file's.

codesmells__hotspot_score.name: Hotspot Score
codesmells__hotspot_score.short: Volatility and risk index scaled between 0 and 100.
codesmells__hotspot_score.long: Measures potential development hotspots by multiplying log-scaled Git change frequency log2(commits + 1) by file size. Non-code files and lockfiles are ignored when calculating the maximum score to prevent scale suppression. Component-level hotspots represent the maximum hotspot score of any contained file.

codesmells__static_complexity_score.name: Static Complexity Score
codesmells__static_complexity_score.short: Structural density index derived from size and nesting.
codesmells__static_complexity_score.long: Measures structural complexity as Lines * (1 + averageIndentation). Capping the average indentation multiplier prevents single nested outliers from skewing the metrics, representing overall file nesting density.

complexity__cognitive__max.name: Worst cognitive complexity
complexity__cognitive__max.short: The cognitive complexity of the hardest function to follow.
complexity__cognitive__max.long: Cognitive complexity, as SonarSource defines it, costs one for each break in the linear flow of a function (an if, a loop, a switch, a catch, a ternary, a run of && or ||) and one more for each level it is nested at. Labelled jumps and recursion are not counted. For a group it is the worst of its files.

complexity__files.name: File Count
complexity__files.short: The total number of files in a component or directory. This is the simplest way to measure size and scope.
complexity__files.long:
Counts all source code files matched during the analysis.
Helpful for understanding component scale and distributing resource metrics.

complexity__files__generated.name: Generated Files
complexity__files__generated.short: Files a tool wrote, by the account of their own header.
complexity__files__generated.long:
Recognised by the markers tools write verbatim: `<auto-generated>` in .NET, Go's
`// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.`, the protocol buffer compiler's header and Django's
migration header. Generated code is part of the build, so it keeps its units and dependencies,
but it receives no code-health reading: nobody edits it by hand.

complexity__files__test.name: Test files
complexity__files__test.short: Files that are tests by their ecosystem's convention (src/test, tests/, *_test.go, *.spec.ts, *.Tests projects).
complexity__files__test.long: Counted apart so a component's size can say how much of it is tests. A file has one role -- production, test, generated, third-party or non-code -- recorded in files.role; this counts the test ones.

complexity__files__third_party.name: Third-party Files
complexity__files__third_party.short: Files that are someone else's code carried in the repository.
complexity__files__third_party.long:
Vendored packages (node_modules, vendor, third_party, lib_npm, wwwroot/lib), minified bundles and
well-known libraries such as jQuery or moment.js. They count as files and lines, since they are in
the repository, but declare no units and receive no code-health reading.

complexity__functions.name: Functions
complexity__functions.short: Functions, methods, constructors and closures a language pack found; a closure inside a function counts as part of it.
complexity__functions.long: Every one of them is in the functions view with its length and cognitive complexity.

complexity__functions__complex.name: Complex functions
complexity__functions__complex.long: SonarSource's default threshold. The functions view lists them.

complexity__indentation__avg.name: Average Indentation
complexity__indentation__avg.short: Average indentation depth across all lines in a file.
complexity__indentation__avg.long:
Measures the mean indentation level of all non-empty lines in a file. Higher average indentation suggests code that spends more time inside nested blocks (loops, conditionals, callbacks), which can reduce readability and increase cognitive load.

When aggregated to directory or component level, this metric is averaged across files.

complexity__indentation__count.name: Indentation Count
complexity__indentation__count.short: Total number of indentation units across all lines in a file.
complexity__indentation__count.long:
Sums the indentation level of every non-empty line in a file. This gives a raw measure of structural depth: a file with many deeply nested lines will have a high count even if the maximum depth is moderate.

Useful for comparing overall structural complexity between files of similar size.

complexity__indentation__deep.name: Deeply indented lines
complexity__indentation__deep.short: Lines indented three levels or more.
complexity__indentation__deep.long: The stand-in for complex code in a language no pack parses: code health's fallback deducts for these lines the way it deducts for lines in complex functions elsewhere. Three levels predicted later bug fixes better than four, five or six, and better than the average or the deepest indentation (tasks/code-health/DECISION.md).

complexity__indentation__max.name: Maximum Indentation
complexity__indentation__max.short: Deepest indentation level found in a file.
complexity__indentation__max.long:
Records the maximum indentation depth (number of indentation units) found on any single line in a file. A high maximum indentation indicates deeply nested control flow, which is a strong indicator of complex, hard-to-read code.

When aggregated to directory or component level, the maximum across all files is taken.

complexity__lines.name: Line Count
complexity__lines.short: The number of lines in the file.
complexity__lines.long: Counts the total number of lines in a file by counting newline characters. This is the most basic size metric and is used as an input to other derived metrics like code health and hotspot score.

complexity__lines__code.name: Code lines
complexity__lines__code.short: Lines that hold code: not blank and not only a comment.
complexity__lines__code.long: Counted by a language pack from the file's syntax tree, so a comment is known as a comment. Code health measures size with it.

complexity__lines__complex.name: Lines in complex functions
complexity__lines__complex.short: Lines inside functions whose cognitive complexity passes 15.
complexity__lines__complex.long: What code health's complex-code deduction counts. 15 is SonarSource's default threshold for a function's cognitive complexity.

complexity__lines__nonblank.name: Non-blank lines
complexity__lines__nonblank.short: Lines with anything on them, comments included.
complexity__lines__nonblank.long: Counted by the indentation reader for every text file. Code health measures size with it when no language pack parses the file; a parsed file is measured by its code lines instead.

complexity__lines__test.name: Test lines
complexity__lines__test.long: The lines of the files whose role is test. Against complexity__lines, the share of a component that is tests.

cycles__short__avg.name: Short Cycle Average Size
cycles__short__avg.short: Average length of shortest cycles this component participates in.
cycles__short__avg.long: The mean number of components in the shortest cycles that include this component. Smaller average cycle sizes indicate tight local coupling, while larger cycles suggest broader circular dependency chains.

cycles__short__count.name: Short Cycle Count
cycles__short__count.short: Number of shortest dependency cycles this component participates in.
cycles__short__count.long:
Counts the number of shortest (minimum-length) cycles that include this component in the dependency graph. Cycles indicate circular dependencies, which can make the system harder to understand, test, and deploy independently.

A component with many short cycles is tightly entangled with its neighbors.

cycles__short__max.name: Short Cycle Maximum Size
cycles__short__max.short: Length of the longest shortest cycle this component participates in.
cycles__short__max.long: The maximum number of components in any shortest cycle that includes this component. A high max cycle size indicates involvement in a broad circular dependency chain spanning many components.

git__additions__total.name: Addition Count
git__additions__total.short: Total number of lines added to this file or component across all commits.
git__additions__total.long:
Sums the number of added lines across all commits that touched a file. At the component level, additions from all files are summed.

Combined with deletion count, this reveals the churn profile of a file: high additions with low deletions suggest growth, while balanced additions and deletions suggest refactoring.

git__age_in_days.name: Age in Days
git__age_in_days.short: Days since the file first appeared in the analysed branch's history.
git__age_in_days.long:
Measures how long a file has existed: the number of days between the scan and the oldest commit
that touched it. For a component or directory it is the age of its oldest file. A file with no
recorded history (not committed, or outside a repository) has no age rather than an age of 0.

Combined with commit count and code health, age separates long-lived code that keeps changing
from code that is new.

git__authors__total.name: Author Count
git__authors__total.short: Number of unique authors who modified this file or component.
git__authors__total.long:
Counts the number of distinct commit authors (by email) who have modified a file. At the component level, unique authors across all files are counted.

A high author count may indicate shared ownership or high-traffic code that warrants extra review attention.

git__commits__total.name: Commit Count
git__commits__total.short: Total number of unique commits that modified this file or component.
git__commits__total.long:
Counts the number of distinct git commits that touched a file. At the component level, this counts unique commits across all files in the component (a single commit touching multiple files is counted once).

High commit counts indicate frequently changed code, which is a key input for hotspot analysis.

git__deletions__total.name: Deletion Count
git__deletions__total.short: Total number of lines deleted from this file or component across all commits.
git__deletions__total.long:
Sums the number of deleted lines across all commits that touched a file. At the component level, deletions from all files are summed.

High deletion counts alongside high addition counts indicate active refactoring or rewrites.

git__last_change_age_in_days.name: Days since last change
git__last_change_age_in_days.short: Days between the last commit that touched it and the newest commit scanned.
git__last_change_age_in_days.long: How long code has sat untouched. Counted back from the newest commit in the snapshot, not from the day of the scan, so a dormant repository reads the same whenever it is scanned. A component or directory reads its most recently changed file's. Compare git__age_in_days, which counts from the first commit instead.

git__repository.name: Git Repository
git__repository.short: The git repository root path relative to the analysis root.
git__repository.long: Identifies which git repository a file belongs to. In monorepo setups with multiple nested .git directories, this distinguishes which repository root owns each file.

git__unique_file_changes__total.name: Unique File Changes
git__unique_file_changes__total.short: Number of unique files changed in commits that touched this file or component.
git__unique_file_changes__total.long:
Counts the number of distinct files that were modified alongside this file across all its commits. At the component level, this counts unique files changed in commits that touched any file in the component.

This metric reveals co-change patterns: a high count suggests the file is coupled to many other files at the change level.

graph__betweenness.name: Betweenness Centrality
graph__betweenness.short: How often a component lies on the shortest path between other components.
graph__betweenness.long:
Betweenness centrality measures the fraction of shortest paths between all pairs of components that pass through a given component. Components with high betweenness act as bridges or bottlenecks in the dependency graph.

Removing or modifying a high-betweenness component is likely to disrupt communication between many other parts of the system.

graph__farness_centrality.name: Farness Centrality
graph__farness_centrality.short: Sum of shortest path distances to this component from every component that reaches it.
graph__farness_centrality.long:
Farness adds up, over every component that depends on this one directly or transitively, the
number of hops its shortest dependency path takes to get here. Components that cannot reach this
one are not counted, so a component nothing depends on has a farness of 0: read it together with
the number of components that reach it, not on its own.

graph__harmonic_centrality.name: Harmonic Centrality
graph__harmonic_centrality.short: Sum of 1/distance over every component that reaches this component.
graph__harmonic_centrality.long:
Harmonic centrality adds up the reciprocals of the shortest dependency paths to this component
from every component that depends on it, directly or transitively. A direct dependent adds 1, one
two hops away adds 1/2, and components that cannot reach it add nothing.

It is a sum, not an average: it grows with how many components depend on this one and how close
they are, which makes it a measure of how widely and how directly this component is relied on.

graph__hits__authority_score.name: Authority Score (HITS)
graph__hits__authority_score.short: How much a component is depended upon by important hubs.
graph__hits__authority_score.long: Part of the HITS (Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search) algorithm. A good authority is a component that is depended upon by many good hubs. In a dependency graph, a high authority score indicates a foundational component that provides core functionality relied upon by orchestrating modules.

graph__hits__hub_score.name: Hub Score (HITS)
graph__hits__hub_score.short: How well a component connects to important authorities.
graph__hits__hub_score.long: Part of the HITS (Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search) algorithm. A good hub is a component that depends on many good authorities. In a dependency graph, a high hub score indicates a component that aggregates or orchestrates many important dependencies.

graph__page_rank.name: PageRank
graph__page_rank.short: Importance score based on the dependency graph structure.
graph__page_rank.long:
PageRank assigns a score to each component based on the number and importance of components that depend on it. A component depended upon by many important components receives a higher score.

In a dependency graph, high PageRank indicates a core component that is critical to the system's architecture.

graph__residual_closeness.name: Closeness (Dangalchev)
graph__residual_closeness.short: Sum of 2^-distance over every component that reaches this component.
graph__residual_closeness.long:
Dangalchev's closeness adds 2 to the power of minus the shortest-path length from every component
that depends on this one: a direct dependent adds 1/2, one two hops away adds 1/4, and components
that cannot reach it add nothing. Like harmonic centrality it rewards being depended on closely
by many components, with far dependents counting for much less.

Despite the metric's stored name, nothing is removed from the graph to compute it.

java__class__declarations.name: Java Class Declarations
java__class__declarations.short: The number of class declarations found in your Java files. This measures the total number of classes defined in the codebase.
java__class__declarations.long: The total number of classes defined within the file or component.

java__field__declarations.name: Java Field Declarations
java__field__declarations.short: The total number of fields (variables inside a class) declared in your Java files. This measures how much state or data your classes hold.
java__field__declarations.long:
Fields are variables declared inside a class block.
A very high number of fields in a single class might suggest that the class is taking on too many responsibilities (a God Class or high state complexity).

java__import__declaration.name: Java Import Declarations
java__import__declaration.short: The number of import statements in your Java files. This shows how many external or internal classes your code references.
java__import__declaration.long:
Tracks individual import statements in Java files.
Used to determine imports of a file, excluding ignored packages like standard java.* libraries if configured.

java__jpa__entities.name: JPA Entities
java__jpa__entities.short: The number of JPA entity classes (annotated with @Entity). These classes represent tables in your database and hold database records.
java__jpa__entities.long: JPA Entities are lightweight persistent domain objects. Typically associated with a table in a relational database.

java__method_declarations.name: Java Method Declarations
java__method_declarations.short: The total number of methods (functions inside a class) declared in your Java files. This measures the number of actions your classes can perform.
java__method_declarations.long:
The total number of methods declared in the Java source files.
A large number of method declarations indicates high behavioral size/complexity.

java__spring__beans.name: Spring Beans
java__spring__beans.short: The total number of Spring-managed beans (classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.). These are the building blocks of a Spring app.
java__spring__beans.long:
Sums up all stereotypic Spring component/bean annotations in the component or file.
A high count suggests heavily Spring-managed business or framework layers.

java__spring__components.name: Spring Components
java__spring__components.short: The number of basic Spring component classes (annotated with @Component). These are helper classes that Spring manages for dependency injection.
java__spring__components.long: A generic stereotype for any Spring-managed component when no more specific stereotype (like Service, Controller, or Repository) applies.

java__spring__configurations.name: Spring Configurations
java__spring__configurations.short: The number of Spring configuration classes (annotated with @Configuration). These classes set up and customize the beans and settings in your application.
java__spring__configurations.long: Indicates that a class declares one or more @Bean methods and may be processed by the Spring container to generate bean definitions and service requests at runtime.

java__spring__controllers.name: Spring Controllers
java__spring__controllers.short: The number of Spring controller classes (annotated with @Controller or @RestController). These classes handle incoming web requests and direct them to the right places.
java__spring__controllers.long:
Spring controller classes process HTTP requests, bind user input, and return responses (often JSON or HTML).
A high density of controllers in one area indicates a major API entry-point area.

java__spring__repositories.name: Spring Repositories
java__spring__repositories.short: The number of Spring repository classes (annotated with @Repository). These classes handle talk to the database to save and load your data.
java__spring__repositories.long: Spring repositories encapsulate storage, retrieval, and search behavior, typically wrapping a relational database using JPA or JDBC.

java__spring__request_mappings__delete.name: Spring DELETE Mappings
java__spring__request_mappings__delete.short: The number of DELETE request endpoints (using @DeleteMapping or @RequestMapping with DELETE). These are web entry points used to remove data.
java__spring__request_mappings__delete.long: HTTP DELETE endpoints are used to delete resource representations.

java__spring__request_mappings__get.name: Spring GET Mappings
java__spring__request_mappings__get.short: The number of GET request endpoints (using @GetMapping or @RequestMapping with GET). These are web entry points used to retrieve data.
java__spring__request_mappings__get.long:
HTTP GET endpoints are used to fetch resources.
A high proportion of GET requests indicates a read-heavy controller.

java__spring__request_mappings__patch.name: Spring PATCH Mappings
java__spring__request_mappings__patch.short: The number of PATCH request endpoints (using @PatchMapping or @RequestMapping with PATCH). These are web entry points used to make partial updates to data.
java__spring__request_mappings__patch.long: HTTP PATCH endpoints are used to apply partial modifications to a resource.

java__spring__request_mappings__post.name: Spring POST Mappings
java__spring__request_mappings__post.short: The number of POST request endpoints (using @PostMapping or @RequestMapping with POST). These are web entry points used to create new data.
java__spring__request_mappings__post.long: HTTP POST endpoints are used to submit data to be processed or to create resources.

java__spring__request_mappings__put.name: Spring PUT Mappings
java__spring__request_mappings__put.short: The number of PUT request endpoints (using @PutMapping or @RequestMapping with PUT). These are web entry points used to update or replace existing data.
java__spring__request_mappings__put.long: HTTP PUT endpoints are used to upsert or replace resources.

java__spring__request_mappings__total.name: Spring Request Mappings (Total)
java__spring__request_mappings__total.short: The total number of web endpoints (using @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.) in your application. It measures how many web entry points you have.
java__spring__request_mappings__total.long:
Total number of HTTP endpoints exposed by Spring MVC/WebFlux controllers.
Indicates the size of the application's external API surface.

java__spring__services.name: Spring Services
java__spring__services.short: The number of Spring service classes (annotated with @Service). These classes hold your application's business logic and rules.
java__spring__services.long:
Spring service classes orchestrate domain logic, communicate with repositories, and manage transactions.
They represent the core business layer of your application.

modularity__abstractness.name: Abstractness
modularity__abstractness.short: Ratio of abstract declarations to total declarations in a component.
modularity__abstractness.long:
Abstractness measures the proportion of abstract types (interfaces, abstract classes) relative to all declarations in a component. Range is 0 (fully concrete) to 1 (fully abstract).

Used together with instability to compute distance from the main sequence.

modularity__component__declarations.name: Component Declaration
modularity__component__declarations.short: A mark that defines where a new component starts, such as a package header in Java/Kotlin or a namespace in C#. This helps identify different parts of your code.
modularity__component__declarations.long:
Component declarations establish the logical boundaries of the system. For instance, package headers or namespace definitions.
They are used to map source files into logical components for coupling and architectural analysis.

modularity__component__imports.name: Component Import
modularity__component__imports.short: A connection that brings in code from another component. It shows when one package or namespace relies on another to work.
modularity__component__imports.long:
Component imports represent dependency edges between different parts of the system.
Analyzing these imports allows us to build a dependency graph and calculate coupling metrics like afferent and efferent coupling.

modularity__coupling__afferent.name: Afferent Coupling
modularity__coupling__afferent.short: Number of files in other components that import this component.
modularity__coupling__afferent.long:
Afferent coupling (Ca) counts the files outside this component that import something from it. This
is Robert Martin's definition, which counts the depending classes rather than the depending
packages; for the number of components that depend on this one, see Direct Dependent Count.

A high afferent coupling means much of the codebase leans on this component, so changes to it
cascade widely and it should be stable and well tested.

modularity__coupling__dependencies.name: Direct Dependency Count
modularity__coupling__dependencies.short: Number of components that this component directly depends on.
modularity__coupling__dependencies.long: Counts the number of components that this component has a direct dependency edge pointing to in the dependency graph. Unlike efferent coupling which counts unique coupling relationships, dependencies counts all direct outgoing dependency edges.

modularity__coupling__dependents.name: Direct Dependent Count
modularity__coupling__dependents.short: Number of components that directly depend on this component.
modularity__coupling__dependents.long: Counts the number of components that have a direct dependency edge pointing to this component in the dependency graph. Unlike afferent coupling which counts unique coupling relationships, dependents counts all direct incoming dependency edges.

modularity__coupling__efferent.name: Efferent Coupling
modularity__coupling__efferent.short: Number of files in this component that import another component.
modularity__coupling__efferent.long:
Efferent coupling (Ce) counts the files inside this component that import something from
another component. This is Robert Martin's definition, which counts the depending classes rather
than the packages depended on; for the number of components this one depends on, see Direct
Dependency Count.

Components with high efferent coupling are more exposed to changes in their dependencies.

modularity__distance_main_sequence.name: Distance from Main Sequence
modularity__distance_main_sequence.short: Distance from the ideal balance of abstractness and stability: |A + I - 1|.
modularity__distance_main_sequence.long:
The main sequence is the ideal line where A + I = 1 (abstractness + instability = 1). The distance from this line measures how well a component balances stability with abstractness.

- D = 0: On the main sequence — ideal balance.
- High D near (0,0): Zone of Pain — stable and concrete. Hard to change.
- High D near (1,1): Zone of Uselessness — unstable and abstract. Over-engineered.

modularity__imports__count.name: Imports
modularity__imports__count.short: Import statements in the file, the standard library's and other projects' included.
modularity__imports__count.long: One per module imported; CommonJS require() counts as one. Code health's coupling deduction reads it.

modularity__instability.name: Instability
modularity__instability.short: Ratio of efferent to total coupling: Ce / (Ce + Ca). Range: 0 (stable) to 1 (unstable).
modularity__instability.long:
Instability is calculated as Ce / (Ce + Ca), where Ce is efferent coupling and Ca is afferent coupling.

- I = 0: Maximally stable — the component has no outgoing dependencies. Changes to other components cannot affect it.
- I = 1: Maximally unstable — the component only has outgoing dependencies. It is entirely dependent on others and likely to be affected by external changes.

The Stable Dependencies Principle (SDP) states that components should depend in the direction of stability: unstable components should depend on stable ones.

modularity__types__abstract.name: Abstract Types
modularity__types__abstract.short: The number of abstract types (like interfaces or abstract classes) in a file or component. These are templates that other classes must fill in.
modularity__types__abstract.long:
Abstract types represent extensible points in your codebase.
A high proportion of abstract types allows components to be easily extended without modifying their core logic, promoting the Open-Closed Principle.

modularity__types__total.name: Total Types
modularity__types__total.short: The total number of types (like classes, interfaces, structs, or records) declared in a file or component. It measures how many structural blocks you have.
modularity__types__total.long:
Total types measures the size of a component in terms of raw structural declarations.
It acts as the denominator when calculating abstractness (abstract types / total types).

rules__dotnet__core_must_not_depend_on_p.name: Core must not depend on a plugin
rules__dotnet__core_must_not_depend_on_p.short: In a .NET plugin architecture, plugins may depend on the core; the core must never depend on a plugin.
rules__dotnet__core_must_not_depend_on_p.long:
A plugin architecture is only extensible in one direction. Plugins are built against the core and
may be added or removed without rebuilding it; the moment the core references a plugin by project,
that plugin is no longer optional and the architecture has quietly become a monolith with extra
project files.

nopCommerce makes the shape plain: 40 .csproj files, of which thirty are named Nop.Plugin.*, and
every one of them references Nop.Web.Framework or Nop.Web rather than the other way round. The
namespaces do not say which module is a plugin, so this rule is checked against the project
references, which do.

rules__go__internal_must_not_be_imported.name: internal must not be imported from another module
rules__go__internal_must_not_be_imported.short: Go's internal/ is a boundary the compiler enforces, so an edge across one is stronger evidence than any ordinary import.
rules__go__internal_must_not_be_imported.long:
A Go package under `internal/` may only be imported by code rooted in the directory holding that
`internal/`. The compiler refuses anything else, which makes it the one boundary in any surveyed
ecosystem that cannot be broken by accident and cannot be argued with.

That is exactly why it is worth reporting. An edge that crosses one did not come from a
language the analyser misread; it came from two modules that were vendored, copied or merged, and
it marks the seam. Within a single module the rule can never fire, so a violation here always
means more than one module is involved.

rules__symfony__component_must_not_depen.name: Component must not depend on Bundle
rules__symfony__component_must_not_depen.short: A framework-agnostic component must never depend on the framework glue that integrates it.
rules__symfony__component_must_not_depen.long:
Symfony projects that separate Component from Bundle do so to keep the domain usable without the
framework: the Component holds the model and the behaviour, the Bundle wires it into Symfony's
container, routing and configuration. The dependency runs one way. A component that reaches back
into its bundle can no longer be used, tested or published on its own, which is the only reason
the split exists.

Sylius is 60 composer packages arranged exactly this way, with 344 interfaces to 663 classes in
its Component tree. The split is declared in composer.json, not in any namespace, which is why
this rule is checked against the module map.
